title: Lal Ded at the table
hookLine: a heaped plate, an empty one, and a proud faster: Lal Ded and the Gita on why a Hindu fast is for God, not for the score
carry: in measure, without pride: the gita's middle road
tomorrow: Gargi asks what everything is woven on.

cards: In plenty of Hindu homes, someone is fasting this week. A Monday fast for Shiva. Ekadashi, the eleventh day of the moon, for Vishnu.
Nine nights of Navratri for the Goddess. Fasting runs all through this faith. So here's a fair question: is the person who eats least the most spiritual one at the table?
Lal Ded, the Kashmiri poet-saint we've spent four days with, has a short saying that catches the overeater and the proud faster at once, and then points to a door.

teach.b: Here is the vakh, in paraphrase. Eat and eat, and you'll get nowhere.
Stop eating, and you'll grow proud. Eat in measure, and you'll become even, and the bolted doors will open. The first line is easy to hear.
The second has the sting. Not eating doesn't make you holy. It can make you proud.
Lal Ded wandered as a seeker and knew the hard road. Of all people, she could have praised it. Instead she warns that it has its own trap: being pleased with yourself for how little you need.
Then the middle: eat in measure, become even, and the bolted doors swing open. She doesn't say which doors; many readers hear the doors within.
The Bhagavad Gita has a neighbor to this saying, in paraphrase: yoga isn't for the one who eats too much, nor for the one who doesn't eat at all.
Elsewhere it says it plainly: evenness is called yoga. Here's the teaching under both.

teach.h: A VRAT IS FOR GOD, NOT THE SCORE
teach.b: In Hinduism a fast, a vrat, is a vow offered to God, not a contest. And the ego, ahamkara, the voice that says look what I did, can feed on anything, even on going without.
That's why Lal Ded aims at the pride, not the hunger.

how: Lal Ded's vakhs, this one among them, are recited and sung in Kashmiri; in many Hindu homes the Gita's brahmarpanam verse is said before meals.

o: a poet who taught eating in measure, not too much or too little
a saint who said a full stomach is the surest road to God
a Kashmiri cook whose dishes are still served at festivals

games.q: Lal Ded at the table — tap the pairs.

s: Lal Ded taught that the less you eat, the holier you are
she warns that not eating can make you proud.
in her saying, eating in measure makes you even, and the doors open
the middle is where the bolted doors swing open.
in Hinduism, a fast is meant as a vow offered to God, not a contest
a vrat is kept for God; Lal Ded warns that pride can sneak in anyway.

games.q: it's monday, and your family keeps a fast for Shiva. a cousin skips water too and keeps telling everyone. by Lal Ded's saying, what fits?
o: keep the fast quietly, in measure, as a vow to God.
go further than your cousin, to show you mean it.
drop it; fasting is just dieting with extra steps.
games.why: too much gets you nowhere, too little can make you proud. a vrat is offered to God and kept evenly; nobody needs the score.

practice: Before your next meal, or now with a glass of water, pause before the first bite or sip.

Many Hindu families say a verse from the Gita here, brahmarpanam, offering the food to God before eating it, so the meal is about who it's for, not more or less. Look at what's in front of you: not heaped, not empty, enough.
If you pray, offer it silently; if you don't, take one slow bite and notice that it's enough.

wordCard.voice: Lal Ded. The poet who said eating too much gets you nowhere, not eating makes you proud, and eating in measure opens the bolted doors. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: in measure, without pride, the Gita's middle road. Not heaped, not empty. Rest well.
